540.title: Tulsidas at Ram Ghat
540.hook: a poet waits by the river to see Rama, and pilgrims still walk barefoot around the hill
540.carry: keep the holy at the center
540.tomorrow: what does Rama tell Sita on the mountain?
540.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Chitrakoot bathe at Ram Ghat on the Mandakini and walk the parikrama around Kamadgiri hill, often barefoot, keeping it on their right; in temples, worshippers circle the inner shrine the same way.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the house of leaves at Chitrakuta, and your line, griha pravesha: bless the home, then enter. Valmiki welcomed the exiles into his own story.
screen: `GRIHA PRAVESHA: BLESS THE HOME, THEN ENTER.`

segments.voice: Most stories happen in places you can't go. Nobody can buy a ticket to Middle-earth. But on the border of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh there's a small town called Chitrakoot, with a green hill, a river and a lot of temples. Every day pilgrims arrive, take off their shoes, and start walking around the hill where, they believe, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana once lived in a hut of leaves.
screen: `PLACES YOU CAN'T GO.` → `A TOWN CALLED CHITRAKOOT.` → `PILGRIMS TAKE OFF THEIR SHOES.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Chitra means bright, many-colored; kuta means a peak. The bright peak. Valmiki names its river, the Mandakini, and it still runs through the town, past the main bathing place, Ram Ghat. Now a story the town tells about itself. The poet Tulsidas, who retold the Ramayana in Hindi, longed to see Rama with his own eyes. A well-loved tradition says Hanuman told him where to wait: Chitrakoot. So he sat at Ram Ghat, grinding sandalwood paste for the pilgrims' foreheads. A boy came and asked for a mark of sandal paste. Tulsidas handed it over and went back to work. He didn't look up. In the telling, Hanuman, as a parrot in a tree, sang out a verse to wake him, and Tulsidas looked up into Rama's face. Tellings differ, but in many, Rama himself puts the mark on the poet's forehead. The story carries a Hindu teaching: God can be standing right in front of you, at an ordinary riverbank, asking for something small. That's why Hindus call some places tirthas, crossing places, where the holy has touched the earth. And they honor them by walking around them. Pilgrims circle Kamadgiri, the hill at the center of town, often barefoot. This is parikrama, also called pradakshina: walking around something holy, keeping it on your right. Many teachers explain it simply: God stays at the center, and your life moves around it. Hindus do the same in temples, circling the inner shrine. So the walk at Chitrakoot isn't sightseeing. It's prayer with your feet. A picture of a whole life: everything moving, God at the center.
screen: `CHITRA AND KUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `TULSIDAS AT RAM GHAT.` · `A BOY ASKS FOR SANDAL PASTE.` · `TIRTHA: A CROSSING PLACE.` · `PARIKRAMA: THE HOLY ON YOUR RIGHT.` · then, large: `KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly around something you hold holy: a home shrine, a tulsi plant, a small lamp. Keep it on your right, the way pilgrims circle Kamadgiri. One circle, or three. If you don't pray, circle something you love, or simply turn once where you stand, and notice what sits at the center of your days.
Chitrakoot, today. A pilgrim town on the Mandakini, where Tulsidas is said to have seen Rama at Ram Ghat, and where people walk barefoot around Kamadgiri, keeping it on their right.

541.title: This mountain is our Ayodhya
541.hook: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
541.carry: dharma kept, the forest is home
541.tomorrow: why can't the old king sleep?
541.howItsDone: In the text, the Mandakini at Chitrakuta is where Rama and Sita bathe; pilgrims to Chitrakoot bathe in the same river today.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot today, and your line, keep the holy at the center. Pilgrims still walk barefoot around Kamadgiri, keeping it on their right.
screen: `KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Every hard story has a pause, a stretch where the characters simply get to live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built. The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night. And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone a neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.
screen: `EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.` → `A RHYTHM TO THE DAYS.` → `SHOWING HER THE NEIGHBORHOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender. Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom. And he gives his reasons. Living here brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy. He takes her down to the Mandakini, where sages bathe with their arms raised to the sun and deer come down to drink. Think of this mountain as Ayodhya, he says, the deer as its people, the Mandakini as our own Sarayu. Here's the teaching. Rama isn't at peace because the forest is pretty. He's at peace because he's doing his dharma, keeping the promise his father made, even at the cost of a crown. That's why Hindus call him maryada purushottama, the best of people, who stays within the bounds of what's right. In the tradition, a word kept doesn't make the forest smaller. It makes it home. And notice who's beside him. Devotees often say his name with hers, Sita-Ram, the two together, as they are on this mountain. One honest note: Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way. We've placed it here because it's the clearest picture of those first days. Now back to Valmiki's order. Far away, the charioteer Sumantra is driving into Ayodhya with an empty chariot. And an old king is waiting.
screen: `I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `HIS FATHER'S WORD, KEPT.` · `MARYADA PURUSHOTTAMA.` · `SITA-RAM, SAID TOGETHER.` · then, large: `DHARMA KEPT, THE FOREST IS HOME.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus repeat Rama's name, often as Sita-Ram, as a quiet practice called japa. If you'd like, say it softly with your breath: Sita on the breath in, Ram on the breath out. If you don't pray, bring to mind one promise you're keeping, even where it costs you, and let each breath out say: this is my part.
Chitrakoot, the happy pause. Rama keeps his father's word, and the mountain, with Sita beside him, becomes their Ayodhya.

542.title: A sound in the dark
542.hook: an empty chariot comes home, and an old king finally tells a secret he has carried his whole life
542.tomorrow: what does the prince do at the hut?
542.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters often tell Dasharatha's confession as its own episode, and later tellings know the young man as Shravan Kumar, in a children's story about care for parents.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot, and your line, dharma kept, the forest is home. Rama kept his father's word, and the mountain became their Ayodhya.
screen: `DHARMA KEPT, THE FOREST IS HOME.`

segments.voice: Sumantra drives back into Ayodhya alone. The horses hang their heads. People look past him into the empty chariot, and then the wailing starts. He gives the king Rama's messages, one by one, and Dasharatha sinks deeper into grief. That night, lying beside Kausalya, unable to sleep, he starts to talk. Not about Rama. About himself, long ago, when he was young and very good with a bow.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT COMES HOME.` → `THE KING CAN'T SLEEP.` → `A STORY FROM LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: He begins with a saying: whatever a person does, good or bad, they eat its fruit later. That's karma, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: every action is a seed, and its fruit comes back to the one who planted it. Then he tells Kausalya what he has never told her. As a young prince, before their marriage, he was famous for one skill. He could hit a target he couldn't see, just by its sound. The Sanskrit word for an archer like that is shabdavedhi, one who pierces by sound. One rainy season, he went out at night along the Sarayu, hoping to catch an elephant coming down to drink. It was dark. He heard a deep gurgling at the water's edge, was sure it was an elephant, fitted an arrow, aimed at the sound, and let go. From the water came a human cry, and a question. Who would shoot at someone like me? I live in the forest, I harm no one, I only came for water. The prince ran to the bank. Half in the river lay a young ascetic with matted hair, an arrow in his chest, and beside him a water pot, the thing that had made the sound. Notice what the old king is doing. He doesn't blame chance for his grief. In the teaching of karma, what comes back isn't random; it grows from what was done, sometimes long after. A skill he was proud of, a guess in the dark, a shot that can't be called back. Tonight, with his son gone, Dasharatha believes the fruit has come.
screen: `WHAT YOU DO, YOU EAT LATER.` · `KARMA: EVERY ACT A SEED.` · `SHABDAVEDHI: HE SHOOTS AT SOUND.` · `A WATER POT, AND A YOUNG ASCETIC.` · then, large: `EVERY ACT BEARS ITS FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or rest them low, and just listen. Notice how fast your mind names each sound, a car, a fan, a voice in the next room, and how fast it wants to act on the name. Let the label go and hear the sound itself. Many teachers say this small gap, before you act, is where the seed of karma is chosen.
Shabdavedhi, one who pierces a target by sound alone. Tonight the old king begins his confession: a shot at a sound in the dark, and a young ascetic at the river.

543.title: The blind parents' curse
543.word: Dasharatha's death and the curse that
543.hook: a prince carries a water pot to a hut where two blind parents are waiting for their son
543.carry: amends begin with telling the truth
543.tomorrow: who was the boy at the river?
543.howItsDone: This episode is often told on its own as a story about duty to parents, and about a prince who told a blind couple the truth instead of slipping away.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: shabdavedhi, and your line, every act bears its fruit. The young prince shot at every act bears its fruit and found a young ascetic with a water pot.
screen: `EVERY ACT BEARS ITS FRUIT.`

segments.voice: The young man in the river doesn't curse Dasharatha. That's the first surprise. He's dying, and what he talks about is his parents. They're old, and both blind, sitting in a hut nearby, thirsty, waiting for me to bring water. Go to them. Tell them. Then he asks one more thing: pull out the arrow. It's burning. The prince knows that if he pulls it, the boy will die. He does it anyway, because he was asked.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CURSE THE PRINCE.` → `MY PARENTS ARE BLIND AND THIRSTY.` → `PULL OUT THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: So Dasharatha fills the pot and walks the path the boy described. At the hut, the old father hears footsteps and speaks first. Why are you so late, son? Your mother was worried. Say something. Picture the prince standing there with the water, mistaken for the son he has just killed. Nobody saw. He could set the pot down and slip away. Instead he tells them everything: who he is, the sound, the elephant he imagined, the arrow. In Valmiki's telling, the father answers with something striking. Because you told us yourself, you are still alive. Had you hidden it, far worse would have followed. The parents ask to be taken to their son. They sit with his body by the river, touching his face, grieving aloud. Then the father speaks the words that will shape Dasharatha's life. Just as I am losing my life in grief for my son, you too will one day die grieving for a son. And the old couple give up their lives on their son's funeral fire. Hold both halves, because Hinduism does. Making amends for a wrong is called prayashchitta, and it starts with owning the wrong out loud. The Manusmriti, one of the old law books, lists confession among its first steps, beside repentance. Telling the truth spared the young prince that night. It didn't cancel the karma. And tonight, with Rama gone and his own life fading, the old king tells Kausalya the curse is coming true.
screen: `WHY ARE YOU SO LATE, SON?` · `HE COULD SLIP AWAY. HE TELLS THEM.` · `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.` · `PRAYASHCHITTA: AMENDS BEGIN WITH THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH SPARED HIM. THE CURSE CAME.`

segments.voice: Think of something small you once got wrong and never quite said out loud, something you can hold gently. Picture telling it plainly to the person it touched, nothing added, nothing hidden. That's where prayashchitta begins. Notice how it feels just to imagine saying it straight.
Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it. The blind father's words: as I die grieving for my son, you too will die grieving for a son.

544.title: Shravan Kumar
544.hook: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes the picture of serving your parents
544.carry: honor mother and father as gods
544.tomorrow: what does a bad dream tell Bharata?
544.howItsDone: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, amends begin with telling the truth. You too will die grieving for a son, the blind father said. The truth spared the prince that night, but not the curse.
screen: `AMENDS BEGIN WITH TELLING THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana. In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture: a son carrying his blind parents on pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders. Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. Here's the surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man has no name, and there are no baskets. Both came later.
screen: `A NAME CHILDREN KNOW.` → `TWO BASKETS ON A POLE.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing; he can't see her anymore. If only Rama would come back and touch me now, he says. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning the attendants come to wake him and find him gone. No son is there for the last rites: Rama is in the forest, and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom. So the ministers lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata comes, and send riders to Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing. Just bring him. Now the boy at the river. Valmiki calls him simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son. Later retellings call him Shravan Kumar and add the pilgrimage, his blind parents carried in two baskets on a pole. Why did a boy with no name become a children's story told across much of India? Because he carries a teaching Hindus hold close. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives a student leaving his teacher these parting words: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you. Caring for your parents, especially as they grow old, isn't only kindness in Hinduism. It's a sacred duty, close to worship. That's why grandparents tell this story at bedtime, and why calling someone a Shravan Kumar is high praise. Even the name fits: shravana is connected with hearing, and this boy was killed by an archer who shot at a sound.

545.title: Bharata comes home
545.hook: riders who won't say why bring a prince home, and his first wish is for his older brother
545.carry: an elder brother stands as a father

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shravana, and your line, honor mother and father as gods. The old king died past midnight, and riders left for Kekaya, saying nothing.
screen: `HONOR MOTHER AND FATHER AS GODS.`

segments.voice: Far away, in his grandfather's city, Bharata wakes up badly shaken. His friends try music and jokes, and he can't smile. He tells them his dream. His father, pale, hair loose, smeared with oil, riding a chariot pulled by donkeys, heading south. In the epics, the south is the direction of Yama, the lord of death. Bharata says: either I, or Rama, or Lakshmana, or the king is going to die. Then the riders from Ayodhya arrive.
screen: `A DREAM IN KEKAYA.` → `A CHARIOT HEADING SOUTH.` → `THE RIDERS ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: The messengers do exactly as they were told. There's urgent business, they say. Come at once. Bharata asks after everyone, one by one: his father, Rama, Lakshmana, the queens. The answers are polite and not quite answers. All is well with those you ask about. So he sets out, days on the road. Then Ayodhya appears, and something is wrong. No music. No crowds. People avoid his eyes. He goes to his father's rooms, and his father isn't there. So he goes to his mother. Kaikeyi is glad to see him, and tells him, almost lightly: your father has gone the way all living things go. Bharata falls to the floor. When he can speak, he asks: where is Rama? I want to touch his feet. He's my father now. That line carries a Hindu teaching about dharma in the family. Later in the Ramayana, Rama himself says that three people are to be honored as fathers: the father, the elder brother, and the one who teaches you. In a traditional Hindu family the eldest brother isn't only a sibling. When the father is gone, he stands in his place, and the younger ones turn to him with a son's respect. You can still hear it at home: a grown man calling his older brother bhaiya and asking him first before a big decision. Bharata's first thought isn't the crown. It's the brother who is now his father. Then Kaikeyi, sure she's giving good news, tells him the rest: the two boons, the exile, the throne kept for him. She thinks she's made her son a king. He only wanted his brother.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-FORTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, an elder brother stands as a father. Bharata came home, asked first for Rama, and Kaikeyi told him the throne was his.
screen: `AN ELDER BROTHER STANDS AS A FATHER.`

segments.voice: Kaikeyi has been waiting for this conversation: her son home, the crown ready. What she gets is fury. Bharata doesn't thank her. He tells her she has destroyed the family, killed his father with grief, and sent away the brother he loves. The kingdom she won for him, he says, he will never accept. Then he walks out, to face the person he dreads most: Kausalya, Rama's mother.
screen: `NO THANKS, ONLY GRIEF.` → `I WILL NEVER ACCEPT IT.` → `NOW, KAUSALYA.`

segments.voice: Kausalya has every reason to suspect him. Here is the son who gains everything from her son's exile. She says so, bitterly: you wanted the kingdom, now you have it. Bharata falls at her feet and swears. Valmiki gives him a long chain of oaths, each naming a wrong he'd rather be guilty of than this. May I carry the guilt of one who betrays a trust, who strikes a sleeping person, who turns away a guest, if I ever wanted Rama gone. Kausalya believes him. She takes his head in her lap, and they weep together. Then the duty that can't wait. Under Vasishtha's guidance, Bharata performs his father's funeral rites, and the family offers water at the Sarayu. That offering, tarpana, water poured from the hands for those who have died, is still part of how Hindu families remember their dead. Afterward Shatrughna catches Manthara, the maid who started it all. Bharata stops him: Rama would never forgive us. Here's why Hindus honor Bharata so deeply. A crown was handed to him, the biggest prize there is. But it was won by wronging his brother, and by custom and by dharma the throne belonged to the eldest, Rama. What comes through adharma, through wrong, isn't worth holding. Bharata's refusal is why the tradition remembers him as the model brother. And so the week closes: a hill, a confession, a curse, a boy who became Shravan Kumar, and a son who put dharma before the crown.
